questions.topic: Feature Pipelines: From Raw Events to Model Inputs
questions.question: What distinguishes a raw event from a feature in an ML data pipeline?
options: An event is numeric and model-ready, while a feature is raw text that still needs encoding before use
An event describes a user, while a feature describes an item, and pipelines exist to join the two records
An event is an immutable record of a fact, while a feature is a derived value for an entity at an as-of time
An event lives on disk in a warehouse, while a feature is always computed in memory at the moment of the request

questions.topic: Feature Pipelines: From Raw Events to Model Inputs
questions.question: In a feature pipeline, why does validation run before transformation and aggregation rather than after?
options: It quarantines malformed or out-of-range events before they can silently corrupt every downstream aggregate
It compresses events into a compact columnar format so the transformation stage can scan far less data
It rewrites event timestamps into processing time so windowed aggregation can run without a clock source
It removes duplicate entity keys so that aggregation windows never count the same entity more than once

questions.topic: Feature Pipelines: From Raw Events to Model Inputs
questions.question: A nightly job that computes daily click counts crashed midway and was re-run; downstream counts for that day are now doubled. Which pipeline defect explains this?
options: The job uses event time instead of processing time, so late clicks were assigned to the wrong day's window
The job appends its output on each run instead of overwriting the day's partition, so it is not idempotent
The job reads from the online store instead of the raw event log, so it aggregated already-aggregated values
The job validates events after aggregation instead of before, so malformed click events were counted twice

questions.topic: Feature Pipelines: From Raw Events to Model Inputs
questions.question: A model is retrained weekly on a 30-day purchase aggregate, and predictions are generated once per night in batch. Which pipeline style fits best?
options: A streaming job that updates the aggregate per event, since incremental updates always cost less than recomputes
A streaming job with a batch backfill, since 30-day aggregates cannot be recomputed inside one nightly window
A request-time computation of the aggregate, since precomputing values for every entity wastes storage
A scheduled batch job that recomputes the aggregate, since nothing consumes values fresher than the nightly run

questions.topic: Feature Pipelines: From Raw Events to Model Inputs
questions.question: Click events can arrive up to 48 hours late. A daily-counts job is re-run three days after its first run and produces different totals. Which design makes re-runs reproducible?
options: Switching the job to processing-time windows so each event is counted in whichever run first observes it
Windowing on event time, waiting out the 48-hour lateness horizon, then treating the partition as immutable
Storing the counts in the online store so that the latest write always replaces any earlier disagreeing value
Deduplicating events by entity key so that late arrivals collapse into rows that were already counted

questions.topic: Feature Pipelines: From Raw Events to Model Inputs
questions.question: A fraud model needs a card's transaction count over the last 10 minutes, served within 50 ms, plus the cardholder's account age. How should each feature be produced?
options: Maintain the 10-minute count incrementally with a streaming job; derive account age from the stored signup date
Recompute both features in a nightly batch job, since consistent snapshots matter more than freshness for fraud
Compute both features at request time by scanning the raw transaction log, since fraud tolerates no staleness at all
Maintain account age with a streaming job and compute the 10-minute count nightly, since counts change slowly

questions.topic: Feature Stores: Offline Training vs Online Serving
questions.question: Why do feature stores maintain both an offline store and an online store rather than a single database?
options: Because training data must be encrypted at rest while serving data has to stay decrypted for fast reads
Because regulators require historical values to be kept apart from any system used in live decisions
Because training scans long histories in bulk while serving needs millisecond point reads
Because feature definitions differ between training and serving, so each path requires its own storage schema

questions.topic: Feature Stores: Offline Training vs Online Serving
questions.question: What does the online store of a feature store typically hold?
options: The full history of every feature value, partitioned by date for efficient training scans
The raw event stream, so serving code can compute any feature on demand from source facts
The model's recent predictions, cached by entity key so repeated requests can skip inference
The latest feature values keyed by entity id, readable in a few milliseconds per request

questions.topic: Feature Stores: Offline Training vs Online Serving
questions.question: An API must assemble 40 features about a user within a 20 ms budget; most are aggregates over 90 days of events. Which design meets the budget?
options: Precompute the aggregates in pipelines and serve them from a key-value online store with a single point read
Issue the 90-day aggregation queries against the warehouse at request time with a strict per-query timeout
Cache the raw events in memory at the API layer and aggregate them inside the request handler on each call
Shard the warehouse by user id so each request-time aggregation query touches only a single partition

questions.topic: Feature Stores: Offline Training vs Online Serving
questions.question: A feature store's registry keeps exactly one definition per feature: its name, entity, source, and transformation. Which failure does this primarily prevent?
options: Storage bloat from materializing the same feature into both the offline store and the online store
Divergence between independently written training and serving implementations of the same feature
Slow training scans caused by feature history being stored row-wise instead of in a columnar layout
Entity key collisions when two teams register features about the same user under different names

questions.topic: Feature Stores: Offline Training vs Online Serving
questions.question: A `spend_30d` feature is refreshed nightly into the online store with a 24-hour TTL. A pipeline outage delays the refresh by 12 hours. What do serving reads see after the TTL expires?
options: The previous value, because online stores retain the last write until a newer write replaces it
The offline store's value, because reads transparently fall back to the historical store on expiry
A recomputed value, because TTL expiry triggers the store to re-derive the feature from raw events
A missing value, so the model receives whatever default the serving code substitutes for the feature

questions.topic: Feature Stores: Offline Training vs Online Serving
questions.question: A team scores all 200k customers once per night and writes results to a table an app reads; there is no request-time inference. How much does a full feature store add here?
options: Considerable value, because nightly scoring requires point-in-time feature retrieval at millisecond latency
Considerable value, because without an online store the nightly job cannot access historical aggregates
Little value, because with no request-time inference nothing needs low-latency online feature lookups
Little value, because 200k customers is too few rows for an offline store to be worth partitioning by date
